hook: In nineteen eighty-three, a passenger jet ran out of fuel at forty-one thousand feet.

blocks.narration: In nineteen eighty-three, a passenger jet ran out of fuel at forty-one thousand feet. The cause was a simple unit mix-up.
blocks.visual: Cinematic storybook illustration of a jet cruising above clouds at sunset, dramatic light

blocks.narration: Air Canada Flight one forty-three was a brand new Boeing seven sixty-seven, one of the first planes in the fleet to use metric units.
blocks.visual: Illustrated gleaming new jet on a tarmac with ground crew holding clipboards

blocks.narration: The fuel gauge was faulty, so the crew calculated fuel by hand. But the math used pounds where it should have used kilograms.
blocks.visual: Illustrated hands scribbling numbers on paper, two unit labels swapping places

blocks.narration: The plane took off with roughly half the fuel it needed. Over Manitoba, warning alarms sounded and then both engines went silent.
blocks.visual: Inside an illustrated cockpit, warning lights flash red and the cabin dims

blocks.narration: By luck, Captain Robert Pearson was an experienced glider pilot. He turned a sixty-ton airliner into the world's biggest glider.
blocks.visual: The silent jet glides through golden clouds with no engine trails

blocks.narration: First Officer Maurice Quintal remembered a former air base at Gimli. It had been turned into a drag racing strip.
blocks.visual: Illustrated old runway with race cars and families gathered on a summer evening

blocks.narration: Coming in too high and fast, Pearson used a sideways slipping maneuver to lose height, then landed hard on the old runway.
blocks.visual: The jet tilts sideways in a dramatic slip, then touches down in a spray of sparks

blocks.narration: All sixty-nine people on board survived, and the plane flew again. Follow for more true stories that sound completely made up.
blocks.visual: Passengers slide down emergency chutes as the sun sets, camera pulls back

captions.hook_line: A passenger jet ran out of fuel at 41,000 feet because of a unit mix-up ✈️
captions.body: On July 23, 1983, Air Canada Flight 143 ran out of fuel mid-flight after a fuel calculation mixed up pounds and kilograms. Captain Robert Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, glided the Boeing 767 to a former air base at Gimli, Manitoba. All 69 people aboard survived.
